Hammurabi revolutionized civilization when he codified his Law for Babylon on stone stelae, enabling all the people to see for themselves what laws bound them (and what punishments would await them if they failed to comply). It has been said that injustice can be defined by codifying the law, but then hanging it too high for anyone to read.

On the one hand, something similar to this has resulted from "codifying" Voat's anti-vote manipulation law within metrics that are unknown to all except Putt who wrote them. On the other hand, revealing the nature of the metrics would render the metrics useless, because those who manipulate votes would then understand what parameters they would need to fall without in order to avoid being detected. Revealing the specifics of the metrics would enable vote manipulators to achieve their ends by simply mimicking what Putt determines to be "organic" voting behaviour.

Let's say Putt, after analyzing how many votes comments (or users) ordinarily accrue over a period of time, judged that a certain rate of votes/minute applies. He then sees one user doubling this base rate within an hour; that user gets flagged for vote manipulation and is warned, and the second or third time, they are banned (after the flagged users are checked by multiple people). Well, if Putt told us that upvoting one user 20 times within one minute (a rate of 20 votes/minute) would be double the evidence-based "typical / organic" rate of 10 votes/minute, and that doubling the base rate is grounds for being flagged, then all the vote manipulators would have to do to avoid ever being flagged is make sure they never upvote (or downvote) a user more than 15 times per minute.

This is just an example of one possible metric (votes per minute) out of an unknown multitude that likely contribute to the flagging of users.

So we're stuck between a rock and a hard place. Two days ago several users were banned (some of whom I considered and still consider to be great users who often offered insightful comments and participated organically within discussions) for "vote manipulation" and almost none of them (I have to presume; they can't tell us because new account registrations are turned off) understand exactly what behaviour got them banned. Isn't this injustice? Is it necessary injustice? Is any injustice ever "necessary"? I do not believe so.

What is the solution, then? Voat has to try to protect the sanctity of votes, not just because votes are how we organize our content (and are supposed to indicate what the real community likes most), but also because Voat makes special use of CCP as an indicator of whether users have "earned" certain privileges, like downvoting, posting submissions, and one day even upvoting. So it's pretty important that upvotes are genuine. But it's also important that users who have been here for years don't wake up one day to find themselves banned for reasons they don't understand.

In my opinion this situation can be handled in a way that protects the sanctity of votes without removing people's long-time accounts or their ability to use Voat whatsoever. My suggested course is in the comments.

Finally we have to consider: if the metrics are such that ordinary users voting a little faster or a little more frequently than usual are getting banned, the metrics probably have to change. Community input might help with this. It's also questionable whether we can treat multiple users all voting against a specific user as manipulation because, to put it frankly, sometimes users are just being faggots and lots of people are seeing their faggotry.

Something has to change. Putt knows more about the metrics than any of us, so he has more reason to have faith in them than the rest of us, but he as a fallen human is also going to be prone to some amount of bias, and those who were banned by the metrics are also going to be prone to their own bias.
